title: The minister who left
hookLine: Emerson resigned his pulpit, unable in conscience to lead communion as the church required

lines: A SERMON THAT WILL COST HIM.
cards: A young minister climbs into his pulpit with a sermon he knows will cost him his job. The people in front of him know him well.
And he's about to explain, carefully and politely, why he can no longer lead one of the central rites of his church, the Lord's Supper, in the way it asks. He isn't angry or storming out.
He's found something he can't do with a clear conscience. His name is Ralph Waldo Emerson, and a new block starts with him walking down from that pulpit.

teach.h: THE LORD'S SUPPER, A SACRED MEAL.
teach.b: First, what was asked of him. In Christian churches, the Lord's Supper, or communion, is a sacred meal, done in memory of Jesus.
Churches understand it in different ways, and for those who receive it, it can be at the heart of their faith. Emerson's church expected its minister to lead it. Second, what he came to think.
In his farewell sermon, Emerson reads the Gospel accounts closely and argues that Jesus did not mean this meal to be a fixed rite for all time.
That's his reading; Christians across the churches have read the same passages very differently, and still do.
Then he goes further, and the further part is personal: this way of remembering Jesus no longer suits him, and for him that is reason enough to give it up. Third, how he left.
By the usual account, he first asked whether he could stay on without leading the rite. The church said no, so he went.
In the sermon he is careful to say he has no hostility to the practice, and no quarrel with those who find it helpful. Fourth, the cost.
A pulpit was his work, his income, his place in the town, and he gave it up over one thing he couldn't do honestly.
That's what in conscience means: not that you're certainly right, but that you won't stand up in front of people and act out what you don't hold.
Most weeks the stakes are smaller: a meeting where you're asked to agree, a form that wants a yes.

how: Readers of Emerson often point to his farewell sermon on the Lord's Supper as an example of leaving a role quietly over a matter of conscience, without attacking those who stay.

games.q: what does “the minister who left” mean?
o: a pastor fired by his church for breaking its rules
a preacher who quit to start a new church of his own
Emerson, who left his pulpit over a rite he couldn't lead

games.q: the minister who left: tap the pairs.

s: Emerson attacked people who took communion
he said he had no hostility to the practice and no quarrel with those who found it helpful.
by the usual account, he asked to stay without leading the rite
the church said no, so he left.
in conscience means being certain you're right
it means not acting out, in front of people, what you don't hold.

games.q: you're Emerson. you can no longer lead the Lord's Supper with a clear conscience, and your church needs you to. what do you do?
o: lead it anyway and keep quiet.
ask to stay without leading it, and leave when they say no.
preach against communion until they fire you.
games.why: by the usual account he asked to stay without leading it. when the church said no, he gave a careful farewell sermon and stepped down.

practice: Ask yourself quietly: is there something I wouldn't do, or wouldn't pretend, even if it cost me a job, a friendship, a good opinion? It might be large, or small, like not laughing at a cruel joke.
Don't argue for it; just find it, name it in a few words, and notice how it feels to hold it.

wordCard.voice: The minister who left. Emerson, who stepped down from his pulpit rather than lead a rite he could no longer lead with a clear conscience, and who said he had no quarrel with those who kept it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: in conscience. Emerson walked out without asking anyone else to follow him. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: The Lord's Supper (farewell sermon at the Second Church, Boston): reading of the Gospel accounts; the rite no longer suitable to him, reason enough to abandon it; no hostility to the institution
